strengths: Novel and insightful perspective: The paper identifies the initial token (attention sink) as a natural, task-agnostic control knob for inference-time attention tuning, avoiding the need for complex task-specific token extraction.

Solid theoretical and mechanistic justification: The authors cleanly demonstrate that scaling the initial token attention modulates the sharpness/smoothness of attention across subsequent tokens while strictly preserving their relative proportions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is tested across 15 diverse benchmarks (text classification, multi-choice QA, and multi-turn chat) and multiple LLM families (Llama-3.1, Qwen-2, DeepSeek-R1), showing consistent performance improvements over vanilla inference and prior attention-steering baselines (ACT, AutoPASTA).

Extensive robustness and ablation studies: The paper provides in-depth investigations into layer-wise impacts, head behavior heterogeneity, resource constraints, varying context lengths, few-shot settings, quantization levels, and decoding strategies.
weaknesses: Reliance on labeled calibration data: ZeroTuning requires ground-truth labels on a calibration set (500 samples) to classify heads as up- or down-effective and select scaling factors. In many practical deployment scenarios, having 500 labeled domain examples may not be readily available, reducing the training-free advantage.

Unclear profiling methodology for open-ended generation: The paper does not clearly specify how head behavior profiling and gamma optimization were performed for open-ended generation tasks such as MT-Bench, where discrete accuracy metrics are unavailable.

Missing comparison with attention temperature tuning: Since scaling the attention sink mathematically modulates the sharpness or entropy of the attention distribution across remaining tokens, comparing ZeroTuning against a standard attention softmax temperature baseline across layers would help isolate whether the effect is uniquely tied to the initial token or to general attention sharpness regulation.

Limited cross-task transferability evaluation: The paper does not evaluate whether the head profiles (up-effective vs. down-effective) identified on one dataset can transfer to another related dataset within the same domain without re-running the profiling step.

strengths: Novel and insightful perspective: The paper identifies the initial token (<BOS>/attention sink) as a universal, task-agnostic control point to modulate attention distribution (sharpening or flattening attention across non-initial tokens) at inference time without needing training or external token-selection models.

Solid theoretical and mechanistic grounding: The authors provide clear derivations showing how scaling the attention score or key states of the initial token regulates attention dispersion across downstream tokens, supported by analysis of layer-wise and head-wise behavioral heterogeneity.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The approach is evaluated across 15 diverse benchmarks (classification, reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and multi-turn conversation via MT-Bench) on four modern LLM architectures (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-13B, Qwen-2-7B, DeepSeek-R1-14B) with various attention implementations (Eager, SDPA, FlashAttention).

Comprehensive ablation and robustness studies: The appendix provides extensive analyses covering resource constraints, context length sensitivity, few-shot settings, decoding strategies, quantization robustness, and prompt perturbations.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on labeled validation data for calibration: The method requires a calibration set (500 labeled validation samples in the experimental setup) to determine optimal scaling factors ($\gamma$) and classify attention heads into up- and down-effective groups. For zero-shot / training-free inference, needing 500 annotated examples per task significantly limits its practical plug-and-play utility.

Computational overhead of head profiling: Iterating through all attention heads (e.g., 32 layers × 32 heads = 1,024 heads in standard architectures) over 500 calibration samples incurs substantial inference cost. As shown in Appendix B, performance drops notably when using resource-constrained setups without full head search (Level 0 vs. Level 2).

Missing comparison to attention temperature scaling: Scaling the sink token essentially sharpens or flattens the attention distribution over the remaining tokens. A crucial missing baseline is direct attention temperature scaling (or head-wise attention temperature scaling), which achieves a similar flattening/sharpening effect without specifically modifying the initial token.

Unclear calibration procedure for generative tasks: While MT-Bench results are reported in Table 3, it is not sufficiently explained how head classification and $\gamma$ selection were performed for free-form multi-turn dialogue where accuracy labels are not available for grid search.

Minor cross-referencing and figure numbering errors: In Appendix F, the text refers to Figure 8 for head proportions, but the corresponding figure is labeled as Figure 7 on page 19, while Figure 8 on page 20 corresponds to quantization.

strengths: Novel angle on attention sinks: The paper provides an interesting empirical perspective connecting the initial token (attention sink) to test-time attention modulation, showing that scaling the attention allocated to the initial token affects the dispersion/concentration of attention over subsequent context tokens.

Comprehensive empirical investigation: The authors conduct extensive diagnostic experiments exploring layer-wise sensitivity (shallow vs. deep layers) and head-level heterogeneity (up-effective vs. down-effective heads).

Breadth of evaluation: The empirical study evaluates multiple model families (LLaMA-3.1, LLaMA-2, Qwen-2, DeepSeek-R1) across a diverse range of benchmarks, including text classification, multiple-choice QA, and multi-turn chat (MT-Bench), supported by extensive ablations in the appendix (context length, decoding strategies, quantization).
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on supervision despite claiming to be a lightweight 'training-free' method: While the model weights are not updated, ZeroTuning requires a labeled validation set of 500 examples per dataset to profile each attention head (evaluating up- vs. down-effectiveness) and to search for the optimal scaling factor gamma. In typical few-shot or zero-shot inference setups, having 500 labeled validation examples constitutes a substantial amount of task supervision, which undermines the practical positioning of the method compared to genuine zero-shot or unsupervised inference-time techniques.

Lack of cross-task transferability and high profiling overhead: The optimal tuning direction varies fundamentally across tasks (e.g., gamma > 1 for SST-2, but gamma < 1 for BoolQ and LogiQA). Without labeled data for a new target task, the user cannot know whether to increase or decrease attention, or which subset of heads to select. Furthermore, sweeping through all attention heads (e.g., 32 layers * 32 heads = 1,024 heads) across 500 validation examples incurs massive inference profiling cost.

Trivial theoretical analysis: The mathematical analysis in Section 2.1 and Appendix A merely restates the basic normalization arithmetic of softmax rescaling when one element in the denominator is scaled. Characterizing this elementary derivation as significant theoretical justification overstates the contribution.

Artificially low vanilla baselines and evaluation setup concerns: Several vanilla baselines report unusually low scores (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct achieving only 73.20% on SST-2, and DeepSeek-R1-14B achieving 27.80% on LogiQA—barely above random chance). This appears to stem from using unconstrained greedy text generation rather than standard constrained decoding or log-likelihood scoring. The reported improvements on classification tasks seem largely driven by fixing formatting/instruction-following failures (e.g., reducing invalid outputs like 'neutral' or 'The') rather than genuine semantic reasoning improvements.

Missing critical calibration baselines: Since the core mechanism adjusts the sharpness or flatness of the attention distribution, the paper lacks comparisons against standard, straightforward attention calibration baselines such as global attention temperature scaling (scaling all attention logits by a temperature tau) or output logit calibration/temperature scaling.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and computationally lightweight idea: instead of relying on external LLM prompts or heuristic rules to identify task-specific salient tokens, the method modulates the attention score/logit of the universal initial token (<BOS>), which naturally acts as an attention sink.

Solid theoretical insight: the paper cleanly shows that scaling the initial token's attention monotonically controls the sharpening/smoothing of the downstream attention distribution while preserving relative proportions among non-initial tokens.

Insightful empirical analyses: the paper discovers head-level heterogeneity (up-effective vs. down-effective heads), layer-wise sensitivity (shallow and middle layers being most influential), and a striking inverse correlation between output entropy and downstream accuracy, enabling an unsupervised calibration mode.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation: tested across 15 benchmarks (text classification, multiple-choice QA, multi-turn conversation), four model families (Llama-3.1, Llama-2, Qwen-2, DeepSeek-R1), and various realistic settings (long contexts, quantization, decoding schemes, and few-shot).
weaknesses: Calibration overhead: Although inference modification takes just a few lines of code, finding the head mask and optimal scaling factor gamma requires a calibration phase (evaluating heads and gamma values across 500 validation examples or sweeping across the test set for entropy minimization), which diminishes the plug-and-play nature for single-sample inference.

Disproportionate gains on format/calibration-sensitive tasks: A significant portion of the large gains in zero-shot classification (e.g., +18.4% on SST-2) appears to stem from preventing invalid or out-of-domain token generation (such as outputting 'neutral' or failing to follow binary format constraints, as detailed in Appendix E.1 and J). On tasks with structured multi-choice options or in few-shot settings, the margins of improvement are much more modest (e.g., 1–3%).

Fragility of key-state modulation under FlashAttention: In optimized kernels where direct attention map modification is unavailable, scaling key vectors introduces exponential sensitivity (exp(gamma * z_0)). As acknowledged in Appendix G, the performance cliff is steep, making manual or grid search for gamma much more brittle in FlashAttention environments.

Minor presentation polish issues: The abstract cuts off mid-sentence at the very end ('Our code and runnable demo are available a'); Figure numbering has minor inconsistencies in the appendix (e.g., Figure 18 appearing twice with different contents on pages 29 and 30).

strengths: Simple and elegant concept: Leveraging the initial token (attention sink) as a task-agnostic lever to control the attention distribution across non-initial tokens is intuitive, computationally lightweight, and requires minimal lines of code.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors validate the method across 15 diverse benchmarks, four model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-13B, Qwen-2-7B, DeepSeek-R1-14B), and multiple configurations (few-shot, long-context, quantization, and alternative decoding strategies).

Effective unsupervised calibration: Introducing an output entropy minimization strategy to identify optimal scaling parameters without labeled validation sets significantly improves the practical utility of the method.

Thorough mechanistic analysis: The paper provides insightful analyses regarding layer-wise impacts, head heterogeneity (up-effective vs. down-effective heads), and clear boundaries of efficacy (e.g., resolving low-confidence uncertainty vs. ingrained factual errors).
weaknesses: Baseline performance sensitivity and formatting artifacts: In several text classification tasks, the vanilla zero-shot baselines are remarkably low (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B on TREC at 14.0%, SUBJ at 44.6%, SST-2 at 73.2%). As qualitative examples in Appendix F and discussions in Appendix E.1 show, the model often outputs explanations or unconstrained tokens (e.g., 'neutral'). It appears a significant portion of the large classification gains stems from suppressing out-of-format generations rather than fundamental improvements in reasoning.

Modest gains on complex reasoning and multiple-choice benchmarks: In contrast to classification benchmarks, the gains on core reasoning and knowledge benchmarks (e.g., MMLU +1.4%, PIQA +1.8%) are considerably more modest.

Search and calibration overhead: While training-free, ZeroTuning still requires head profiling and grid-searching for an optimal scaling factor $\gamma$ (either on 500 labeled validation samples or across an unlabeled set via entropy minimization), which introduces computational overhead and limits purely online, zero-context single-query deployment.

Evaluation on reasoning-focused LLMs: DeepSeek-R1-14B is included, but only evaluated on standard zero-shot classification and MCQA benchmarks. It remains unanalyzed how modulating the initial token impacts long chain-of-thought generation dynamics, response lengths, or math/code reasoning (e.g., on GSM8K or MATH).

strengths: Simple and computationally lightweight concept: Modulating the initial token's attention (or its key vector) requires minimal code changes and can be adapted to optimized attention kernels such as FlashAttention and SDPA.

Clear mathematical formulation: Section 3.1 and Proposition 1 clearly show how scaling the initial token's attention score preserves relative proportions among non-initial tokens while scaling their differences, acting as a global smoothing/sharpening factor.
Comprehensive empirical analysis: The authors provide detailed ablation studies across layers, individual attention heads, context lengths, decoding strategies, and quantization levels.
weaknesses: Severely degraded vanilla baselines and flawed evaluation protocol: The reported vanilla baseline accuracies for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct are uncharacteristically poor for standard benchmarks. For instance, in Table 1, LLaMA-3.1-8B achieves only 14.00% on TREC (6-class classification, where random guess is ~16.7%), 44.60% on SUBJ (binary classification, below random guess of 50%), and 73.20% on SST-2. As revealed in the qualitative error analysis (e.g., Appendix E.1 and F), the vanilla model frequently produces out-of-format tokens (such as 'neutral' or explanatory text) under free-form greedy generation. Rather than evaluating standard label-token log-likelihoods (the standard practice in benchmarks like lm-evaluation-harness) or using appropriate constrained decoding, the method appears to gain huge percentage jumps largely by shifting generation back into task-compliant label tokens. This severely undermines the claim of genuine cognitive/reasoning enhancement.

Heavy reliance on per-dataset calibration undermines practical utility: The method requires searching for task-specific scaling factors ($\gamma$) and profiling individual attention heads on a 500-sample labeled calibration set for each dataset. If 500 labeled examples are available per task, standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA) or standard in-context few-shot learning are much more natural choices and typically yield much higher, more stable performance.

Contradictory directional requirements make deployment on general-purpose LLMs problematic: The optimal scaling direction varies drastically across tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis favors up-scaling $\gamma > 1$, while reading comprehension like BoolQ and LogiQA favors down-scaling $\gamma < 1$). In a general-purpose interactive assistant, an LLM handles diverse query types concurrently; applying a single global initial-token intervention that improves one capability would systematically degrade another.

Impractical unsupervised calibration: The proposed unsupervised mode requires sweeping over candidate values of $\gamma$ and finding the minimum average output entropy across the entire unlabeled evaluation set. This setup is inherently offline and transductive, making it inapplicable to standard online, single-prompt inference settings.

Missing standard inference-time and calibration baselines: The comparison is restricted to vanilla decoding, ACT, and Auto-PASTA. The paper lacks comparison against well-established post-hoc output calibration techniques (e.g., Zhao et al., 'Calibrate Before Use') or standard logit-bias/constrained decoding methods that address the exact format compliance issues observed here.
